title: Zanubrutinib-rituximab followed by shortened chemoimmunotherapy as frontline treatment for mantle cell lymphoma (CHESS): a phase II trial

paper_content.abstract: Combination of Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor ibrutinib and rituximab has shown promising efficacy in mantle cell lymphoma (MCL). This phase II trial evaluated the second-generation BTK inhibitor zanubrutinib plus rituximab as induction, followed by shortened chemoimmunotherapy as frontline treatment for MCL (NCT04624958). Eligible patients had histologically confirmed stage II–IV disease requiring immediate therapy and no prior MCL-related systemic treatment. Patients received zanubrutinib-rituximab for up to 12 cycles (part A); those achieving complete response (CR) or experiencing disease progression proceeded to four cycles of R-DHSAOx (rituximab, dexamethasone, cytarabine and oxaliplatin) (part B). Patients with CR after part B received zanubrutinib maintenance for one year. The primary endpoint was the CR rate at part A completion. Forty-two patients were enrolled. The CR rate at part A completion was 88% (95% confidence interval [CI], 74-96), and 86% (95% CI, 72-95) at part B completion. Hematologic toxicities predominated: the most common grade 3-4 adverse events were neutropenia (7%) in part A, and thrombocytopenia (77%) and neutropenia (49%) in part B. In conclusion, zanubrutinib-rituximab induction followed by shortened R-DHAOx is efficacious with manageable safety as frontline therapy for MCL. This strategy allows for a reduction in chemotherapy cycles and warrants validation in randomized controlled trials.
paper_content.introduction:
Mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), a subtype of mature B-cell lymphoma, is characterized by translocation of t(11;14)(q13;q32) and cyclin D1 overexpression.1 The standard of care aggressive therapy for MCL is cytarabine-based chemoimmunotherapy regimens, such as the LyMa regimen (rituximab, dexamethasone, cytarabine, and platinum [R-DHAP] × 4 cycles followed by rituximab, cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, and prednisone [R-CHOP] × 4 cycles in non-complete response [CR] patients),2 the NORDIC regimen (dose-intensified R-CHOP alternating with rituximab and high-dose cytarabine × 6 cycles),3 R-CHOP + ibrutinib alternating with R-DHAP × 6 cycles,4 rituximab and bendamustine (BR) × 3 cycles followed by rituximab and high-dose cytarabine × 3 cycles,5 with optional autologous stem cell transplantation (ASCT) and maintenance therapy. For patients not suitable for aggressive induction therapies and ASCT, several less aggressive regimens without high-dose cytarabine, such as bortezomib, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and prednisone (VR-CAP) regimen,6 BR regimen,7 BR + acalabrutinib regimen,8 are recommended. Although cytarabine plays a significant role in the frontline treatment of MCL, the aforementioned cytarabine-based regimens are associated with significant myelosuppression and an increased risk of secondary malignancies.4,5,9,10

Treatment of MCL has been revolutionized by Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitors during the past decade.11-15 Several trials have shown promising efficacy of combining BTK inhibitors and rituximab as frontline treatment in MCL patients with older age or indolent disease.16-20 In the WINDOW-1 trial, the BTK inhibitor ibrutinib and rituximab as induction therapy followed by shortened R-HCVAD (rituximab, hyper-fractionated cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, and dexamethasone) alternating with R-methotrexate-cytarabine regimen in previously untreated MCL patients resulted in 87% complete response (CR) rate after induction and 89% CR rate after R-HCVAD regimen.21

Compared with ibrutinib, the second-generation BTK inhibitor zanubrutinib has higher selectivity for BTK and thus fewer off-target toxicities.22-24 In comparison to ibrutinib, zanubrutinib demonstrated less cardiovascular toxicity and lower rate of treatment discontinuation with comparable efficacy in phase 3 trials.25,26 In a phase 2 trial for relapsed or refractory MCL, zanubrutinib achieved 78% CR rate and 33-month median progression-free survival (PFS).13 Considering the favorable efficacy and safety profile, using zanubrutinib as a frontline treatment may represent a promising approach.

We conducted this phase II trial (CHESS) to evaluate the safety and efficacy of zanubrutinib plus rituximab as induction therapy, followed by a shortened course of chemoimmunotherapy in previously untreated MCL patients. R-DHAOx regimen (rituximab, dexamethasone, cytarabine, and oxaliplatin) was selected based on its proven efficacy in clinical practice and several key factors: 1) improved outcomes of adding high-dose cytarabine to chemoimmunotherapy;27 2) a high CSR rate (77%) in the LyMa trial with the R-DHA-platinum regimen,2 which is recommended by the National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guideline; 3) a tendency for longer disease control duration observed with oxaliplatin in subgroup analyses of the LyMa trial compared to cisplatin and carboplatin;28 and 4) Given that the potential overlapping toxicity of thrombocytopenia in high-dose cytarabine and carboplatin, as well as lower nephrotoxicity and ease of administration with oxaliplatin than cisplatin,29,30 we chose oxaliplatin as the platinum used in our regimen. In this work, we show that zanubrutinib-rituximab induction followed by shortened chemoimmunotherapy yield promising efficacy and an acceptable safety profile as frontline treatment for MCL. Based on transcriptome features, we identified three molecular subtypes that correlate with treatment response and survival outcomes.
paper_content.results:
Patients
Between December 1, 2020, and December 13, 2023, 42 patients were enrolled. Baseline characteristics are summarized in Table 1. The median age was 57 years (interquartile range [IQR], 51-64), and 35 patients (83%) were male. Based on tumor tissue samples, Ki-67 was ≥ 30% in 29 (69%) patients; histological subtype was blastoid/pleomorphic in 5 (12%) patients. The risk based on the simplified Mantle Cell Lymphoma International Prognostic Index (sMIPI) was low, intermediate, and high in 24 (57%), 15 (36%), and 3 (7%) patients, respectively. Minimal residual disease (MRD) in bone marrow was detected in 36 (86%) patients. In the 35 patients with known MRD status in peripheral blood, the bone marrow and peripheral blood results were concordant except in one patient (positive in bone marrow but negative in peripheral blood) (Supplementary Table 1). In the six patients without bone marrow involvement at baseline, none had detectable MRD in peripheral blood, and they underwent MRD detection only in peripheral blood in subsequent time points.

The study profile is shown in Figure 1. All 42 enrolled patients received part A induction treatment; 39 proceeded to part B chemoimmunotherapy. All 29 patients who completed the 4-cycle part B chemoimmunotherapy, as well as five patients who discontinued part B due to toxicities, received maintenance therapy with zanubrutinib. As of November 20, 2024, 23 patients had finished the study treatment, and 11 were still receiving maintenance therapy.

Response
The median treatment cycle in part A was 4 (IQR, 4-4), and all 42 patients were evaluable for response. For the evaluation of the primary endpoint, 37 (88%; 95% CI, 74-96) patients achieved CR at part A completion. The remaining five patients (12% [95% CI, 4-26]) experienced disease progression (Table 2 and Supplementary Figure 1). CR was confirmed by 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron-emission tomography (PET) in all patients, plus bone marrow biopsy in patients with bone marrow involvement at baseline. Detailed information on the patients with progressive disease (PD) is provided in Supplementary Table 2. The best overall response rate (ORR) and CR rate was 98% (95% CI, 87-100) and 88% (95% CI, 74-96), respectively. The median time to CR was four months (IQR, 4-4). MRD was negative at part A completion in 33 patients (Supplementary Table 1), and the MRD-negative CR rate was 74% (31/42; 95% CI, 58-86). The dynamic change of MRD and its relationship with treatment response are presented in Supplementary Figure 2. In post-hoc subgroup analyses, the CR rate at part A completion was 40% (2/5) in patients with blastoid/pleomorphic disease and 95% (35/37) in those with classic/small cell disease; 33% (1/3) in patients with TP53 mutation and 94% (32/34) in those with wild type TP53. There were no obvious differences in other subgroups, including age, sex, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) performance status, stage, bone marrow involvement, lactate dehydrogenase, Ki-67 and sMIPI risk (Supplementary Table 2).

Thirty-nine patients proceeded to part B treatment with R-DHAOx regimen. At part B completion, among the 39 patients, the CR rate was 92% (36/39; 95% CI, 79-98), and disease progressed in the remaining three patients (8%; 3/39; 95% CI, 2-21; all had PD in part A) (Table 2). Thirty-six of the 37 patients with CR at part A completion remained in CR and had undetectable MRD at part B completion (Figure S2 and Table S1); one patient was lost to follow-up after part A.

For the overall response following part B completion, 36 patients achieved CR (86% [95% CI, 72-95]), three patients had PD (7% [95% CI, 2-20], and three patients were not evaluable due to not receiving part B treatment. In post-hoc subgroup analyses, the CR rate at part B completion was 40% (2/5) in patients with blastoid/pleomorphic disease and 92% (34/37) in those with classic/small cell disease; 33% (1/3) in patients with TP53 mutation and 91% (31/34) in those with wild-type TP53 (Table S2). There were no significant differences in other subgroups.

Survival outcomes
With a median follow-up of 23 months (IQR, 14-29), the median PFS and overall survival (OS) were not reached. The analysis of the median PFS and OS were planned but the data were immature. The 2-year PFS and OS rate was 85% (95% CI, 75-97) and 90% (95% CI, 75-100), respectively (Figure 2A, B). The median duration of response (DoR) was 17 months (IQR, 8-23). Five patients experienced disease progression and three patients died due to lymphoma progression, all were non-CR patients in part A. Detailed clinical information and salvage therapies of the five PD patients in the current trial are summarized in Supplementary Table 3 and Supplementary Table 4. None of the 37 patients with CR at the completion part A had disease progression; one died of COVID-19 pneumonia. Patients with blastoid/pleomorphic disease had inferior survival outcomes than those with classic/small cell disease (Supplementary Figure 3A and Supplementary Figure 4A). Patients with TP53 mutations had inferior PFS, but no OS difference was observed. Neither PFS nor OS differed between the patients with different age (< 60 vs ≥ 60 years), stage (II vs III-IV), Ki-67 (< 30% vs ≥ 30%) or sMIPI risk (low vs intermediate vs high risk) (Supplementary Figure 3 and Supplementary Figure 4).

Adverse events
In part A, the most common treatment-related AEs (TRAEs) were neutropenia (11 [26%] of 42 patients), fatigue (11 [26%]), lymphocytopenia (11 [26%]), and rash (9 [21%]) (Table 3). Hemorrhage (all grade 1 or 2) occurred in four (10%) patients. The most common grade 3-4 TRAEs were neutropenia (3 [7%]) and lymphocytopenia (3 [7%]). No patient needed zanubrutinib dose reduction in part A. Zanubrutinib dose suspension was required in five (12%) of 42 patients (three patients for neutropenia, one for infection, and one for elevated liver enzymes). None of the patients needed recombinant human granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (rhG-CSF) supportive treatment during part A. There were no treatment-related deaths.

In part B, grade 3-4 events were predominantly hematological. The most common grade 3-4 TRAE was thrombocytopenia (30 [77%] in 39 patients), followed by leukocytopenia (23 [59%]), and neutropenia (19 [49%]) (Table 3). The most common non-hematological TRAEs were elevated liver enzymes (20 [51%]) and fatigue (20 [51%]), but most were grade 1-2. Dose reduction of chemotherapeutic agents was required in 32 (82%) of 39 patients due to toxicities (27 patients for thrombocytopenia, four for neutropenia, and one for elevated liver enzymes). Of these, 25 patients had their dose of cytarabine reduced by one dose level to 75% of the original dose, and seven patients required a reduction of two dose levels to 50%.

Thrombopoietin receptor agonists (TPO-RAs) or recombinant human thrombopoietin (rhTPO) were given in 9 patients as primary prevention for thrombocytopenia, and in 13 patients as secondary prevention. Five patients still experienced severe thrombocytopenia despite supportive care with TPO-RAs or rhTPO and dose reduction, and therefore discontinued treatment. rhG-CSF was given in 26 patients as primary prevention for neutropenia, and in all the 19 patients who had experienced grade 3-4 neutropenia as secondary prevention. None of the patients experienced further occurrence of severe neutropenia after receiving rhG-CSF supportive therapy and dose reduction. Chemotherapy dose suspension was required in 20 (51%) of 39 patients due to toxicities (18 patients for thrombocytopenia, one for neutropenia, and one for elevated liver enzymes). Five patients discontinued chemotherapy permanently due to toxicities (all due to grade 4 thrombocytopenia). There were no treatment-related deaths.

TRAEs in the zanubrutinib maintenance phase are summarized in Table 3. One patient experienced grade 3 neutropenia and recovered after supportive treatment with rhG-CSF, after which the zanubrutinib dose was reduced to 80 mg twice daily. No other dose reductions were required during the maintenance phase. Zanubrutinib dose suspension was required in six (18%) of 34 patients (two patients for neutropenia, two patients for fatigue, and one patient each for thrombocytopenia and infections). No patient required treatment discontinuation.

This trial was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic. One patient died from COVID-19 pneumonia and respiratory failure during part B. A total of 30 patients tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 at least once, and 17 patients required treatment suspension due to SARS-CoV-2 infection.

Transcriptional and genomic analyses
Unsupervised hierarchical clustering of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) based on bulk RNA sequencing in 37 available tumor tissue samples at baseline revealed three MCL molecular subtypes (M1-M3) (Figure 3A). M1 (n=4) was characterized by activation of cell-cycle pathways, including G2M pathways, E2F targets, MYC targets and DNA replication (Figure 3B and Figure S5A). M2 (n=26) was characterized by activation and regulation of T cells (T cell activation, T cell antigen processing and presentation, and T cell co-stimulation) and DNA repairing (Figure 3B). M3 (n=7) was characterized by upregulation of inflammatory pathways (e.g., JAK-STAT3 signaling and TNF-α signaling) (Figure 3B and Supplementary Figure 5A). Activation of specific pathways (e.g., hypoxia, angiogenesis, extracellular matrix organization, and cell matrix adhesion) and the increased infiltration of stromal cells and immunosuppressive cells (cancer-associated fibroblasts and myeloid-derived suppressor cells) (Supplementary Figure 5B) indicated a more complex tumor microenvironment in M3. The genomic profiles including mutated genes and tumor mutation burden in each molecular subtype are presented in Supplementary Figure 6.

None of the four patients of the M1 subtype achieved CR in part A; all the four patients experienced PD within 9 months and died within 24 months (Figure 3C, D). In contrast, all patients of the M2 subtype obtained early-CR. In the seven patients of the M3 subtype, two achieved early-CR and the remaining five achieved late-CR (Figure 3C). The distribution of histological subtypes, sMIPI risk, and Ki-67 in different molecular subtypes are presented in Supplementary Figure 5C. In the 24 patients of the M2 subtype with positive MRD at baseline, MRD became undetectable in all 24 patients at the completion of part A. In contrast, the MRD status remained unchanged from baseline to part A completion in all patients of the M1 and M3 subtype (Figure 3E).
paper_content.methods:
Trial design and patients
This trial protocol was approved by the ethics committees of participating centers (ethics committee of Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center, ethics committee of Huizhou Municipal Central Hospital, and ethics committee of the Second Hospital of Dalian Medical University). The trial was conducted according to the Declaration of Helsinki and all relevant regulations regarding the use of human study participants. All patients provided written informed consent. The consent to publish clinical information potentially identifying individuals was obtained. This trial is registered with ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04624958 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04624958; first posted on November 12, 2020).

This investigator-initiated, single-arm, phase II trial (CHESS) was conducted in three centers in China. This was an open-label trial. Participants, investigators, attending physicians and outcome assessors were not blinded. Previously untreated patients aged 18-75 years with histologically confirmed, Ann Arbor stage II-IV MCL, requiring immediate anti-lymphoma treatment were eligible. Additional inclusion criteria included: ECOG performance status score of 0 to 2, at least one measurable lesion, and adequate organ and bone marrow function. Patients were excluded if they had central nervous system involvement, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, history of active bleeding or hemorrhagic diathesis, required treatment with anticoagulants or strong CYP3A inhibitors. The full list of inclusion and exclusion criteria is presented in trial protocol in the supplementary notes.

Study treatment
The treatment consisted of three phases. A treatment schema describing the study treatment process is presented in Supplementary Figure 7. In part A (induction phase), zanubrutinib (160 mg, twice a day, orally) and rituximab (375 mg/m2, intravenously on day 1) were administered in 28-day cycles until CR, disease progression or unacceptable toxicity, with a maximum of 12 cycles. In part B (chemoimmunotherapy phase), R-DHAOx (rituximab 375 mg/m2 intravenously on day 1; dexamethasone 20 mg intravenously on days 1-4; cytarabine 2 g/m2 intravenously on days 2-3 [1 g/m2 for patients > 65 years of age]; and oxaliplatin 130 mg/m2 intravenously on day 1) was administered in 21-day cycles until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity, with a maximum of four cycles. In maintenance phase, zanubrutinib (160 mg orally, twice a day) was given until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity for up to one year. Unacceptable toxicity was defined as meeting any of the criteria for dose discontinuation of zanubrutinib or chemotherapeutic drugs as described in protocol during treatment, or if continued treatment is deemed inappropriate by the investigators.

Patients achieving CR or PD in part A proceeded to part B; patients with PR or stable disease (SD) in part A received 12 cycles of zanubrutinib-rituximab treatment prior to proceeding to part B. Patients with CR at part B completion proceeded to maintenance phase; young patients (≤ 65 years) with detectable MRD were eligible for ASCT before maintenance. Patients with PR, SD or PD at part B completion were taken off the trial.

Assessments and endpoints
Responses were evaluated by the investigators every two cycles in part A and part B, and every three cycles during maintenance therapy using PET or computerized tomography (CT) according to the Lugano 2014 criteria.32 A bone marrow biopsy is required to confirm CR in patients with bone marrow involvement at baseline. Safety assessment was performed upon all patient visits. Adverse events (AEs) were graded according to the National Cancer Institute’s Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (version 5.0).

MRD in bone marrow and/or peripheral blood was measured using flow cytometry with a sensitivity of 10-4 at baseline and upon the completion of part A and part B. Bone marrow aspiration was performed at completion of part A and part B in patients with bone marrow involvement at baseline but not routinely in patients without bone marrow involvement at baseline. The collection of peripheral blood for MRD evaluation was performed at baseline and upon the completion of part A and part B. Detectable MRD in either bone marrow or peripheral blood was considered MRD-positive.

The primary endpoint was the CR rate at the completion of part A in the intention-to-treat population, defined as proportion of patients with CR. Secondary endpoints included overall response (proportion of patients with CR plus PR), MRD, PFS, OS, DoR, time to CR, and adverse events for part A, part B and maintenance phase. PFS was defined as the time from treatment initiation to disease progression or death, whichever occurs earlier, and was censored at the last follow-up date in alive patients without disease progression. OS was defined as the time from treatment initiation to patient death or the last follow-up. DoR was defined as the time from first response to disease progression or death, whichever occurs earlier. Time to CR was defined as the time from treatment initiation to the first documentation of CR.

RNA-seq and transcriptomic analyses
Total RNA from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tumor samples obtained at baseline were extracted using the RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen). RNA purity was assessed using Nanodrop 2000 for A260/280 and A260/A230 ratios (Thermo Fisher Scientific). All RNA samples were quantified by Qubit 3.0 using the RNA BR Assay Kit (Life Technologies). RNA integrity was assessed using Bioanalyzer 2100 (Agilent). RIN value (RNA integrity number) higher than 6.5 was required. RNA sequencing libraries were prepared using KAPA Stranded RNA-Seq Kit with RiboErase (KAPA Biosystems). Final library was quantified using KAPA Library Quantification Kit (KAPA Bio- systems), and sequenced on the Illumina HiSeq4000 platform using PE150 sequencing chemistry (Illumina, USA) to an average of 50 M reads per sample.

FASTQ file quality control was performed using Trimmomatic,39 where N bases and low quality (score < 15) bases were removed. Reads aligning to rRNA and tRNA sequences were removed. Cleaned reads were aligned to the human reference genome (hg19) using STAR v 2.5.2b.40 Transcripts were quantified using RSEM,41 which uses an expectation maximization algorithm to optimally assign reads that maps to multiple transcripts.

Based on treatment response at the completion of part A, we categorized the patients into three groups: early-CR (achieving CR within four cycles of zanubrutinib-rituximab regimen), late-CR (achieving CR after more than four cycles of zanubrutinib-rituximab regimen), and non-CR. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between non-CR, late-CR and early-CR tumors were identified using edgeR package (v4.3.16) with its default parameters. DEGs were defined as genes with |log (fold change)| > 0.5 and P-value < 0.01. RNA-seq data were deconvolved with the ESTIMATE algorithm (v1.0.13) in R software and TIDE algorithm (v1.3) in python 3.12.7 software for immune infiltration analyses.

Samples were classified into three subtypes based on the normalized FPKM values of DEGs by applying an unsupervised hierarchical clustering method. When performing unsupervised hierarchical clustering, we calculated the distance matrix using the Euclidean distance metric (dist function with method = "euclidean") and applied the hclust function with the Ward's minimum variance method (method = "ward.D"), which minimizes the total within-cluster variance. The results were visualized using a dendrogram to represent the hierarchical structure of the clusters. To specify a desired number of clusters, we used the cutree function to cut the dendrogram. To visualize subtype characteristics, a heat map was generated using ComplexHeatmap R package (v 2.21.1) based on normalized FPKM values of DEGs.

Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) of Hallmark and Reactome pathways, and Gene Ontology terms were performed using clusterProfiler R package (v4.13.3) based on pre-ranked differentially expressed gene panels of each subtype. Single-sample GSVA scores of GOBP, Hallmark and Reactome gene sets in the MSigDB database (v2024.1.Hs) were calculated using GSVA R package (v1.53.23) and the representative significantly enriched pathways in the three subtypes were plotted using the pheatmap R package (v1.0.12).

DNA sequencing and genomic analyses
DNA from FFPE tissue and matched germline samples were extracted using a DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (Qiagen). Purified DNAs were quality checked using Nanodrop 2000 for A260/280 and A260/A230 ratios (Thermo Fisher Scientific). All DNA samples were quantified by Qubit 3.0 using the dsDNA HS Assay Kit (Life Technologies). Sequencing libraries were prepared using the KAPA Hyper Prep Kit (KAPA Biosystems). Target enrichment was performed using the xGen Exome Research Panel and Hybridization and Wash Reagents Kit (Integrated DNA Technology, USA) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Libraries were subjected to PCR amplification with KAPA HiFi Hot-Start ReadyMix (KAPA Biosystems). The purified library was quantified using the KAPA Library Quantification Kit (KAPA Biosystems), and its fragment size distribution was analyzed using a Bioanalyzer 2100 (Agilent). Sequencing was performed on Illumina HiSeq4000 platform using PE150 sequencing chemistry (Illumina, USA).

FASTQ file quality control was performed using Trimmomatic,39 where N bases and low quality (score < 20) bases were removed. Pair-end reads were aligned to the human reference genome (hg37) using Burrows-Wheeler Aligner (BWA) with default parameters, followed by PCR deduplication with Picard V2.9.4 (Broad Institute, MA, USA). Local realignment around indels and base quality score recalibration was performed with the Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK 3.4.0). Somatic single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) were identified using VarDict and MuTect2 for matched tumor-normal samples, and Haplotyper2 for tumor-only samples. To eliminate sequencing artifacts and common germline events in tumor-only samples, both SNVs and small insertions/deletions (indels) were filtered using an in-house common variant database that includes 2000 whole-exome sequencing (WES) normal samples. Final list of mutations was annotated using vcf2maf (available on GitHub). Resulting mutation list was filtered through an internal list. Somatic mutation calls were further filtered using the following criteria: (i) minimum 4 reads supporting the variant; (ii) ≥ 2% variant allele frequency (VAF); (iii) not present in public databases (Exome Variant Server, 1,000 genomes project and Exome Aggregation Consortium) at population frequency > 1%; (iv) in protein-coding regions. Oncoprint, constructed by R (3.5.3), was used to view the overall mutation landscape of patients. Tumor mutation burden (TMB) was counted by summing all base substitutions and indels in the coding region of targeted genes, including synonymous alterations to reduce sampling noise and excluding known driver mutations as they are over-represented in the panel.42

Statistical analysis
Sample size was estimated according to a single-stage phase 2 design based on the following assumptions: 1) CR rate of 70% for historical control2 and 90% with the regimen in this trial; 2) 90% power and two-sided 5% type I error; 3) a dropout rate of 10%. The calculation yielded 42 patients. Response assessment was performed in the full analysis set (ITT population) and per protocol set. Safety assessment was performed in the safety analysis sets, which was divided into three datasets and each contained patients who received the study treatment at least once in part A, part B, or maintenance phase. Descriptive statistics were used to present baseline characteristics, response rates, and rate of AEs. The 95% confidence interval (CI) of rates was calculated using the Clopper-Pearson method. Survival outcomes and 95% CIs were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. The 2-year PFS and OS were calculated. The log-rank test was used to evaluate the difference in PFS and OS between subgroups. Post-hoc analyses included the subgroup analyses of CR rate at part A completion, CR rate at part B completion, PFS, and OS. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 25.0), R software (version 3.6.1) and python (version 3.12.7). Two-sided P of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Although the combination described is of interest in MCL and window studies have now been performed with ibrutinib,
acalabrutinib and zanubrutinib, this manuscript lacks depth in the discussion of the study results in the context of the other
trials, including those of BTKi +R bendamustine, R-BTKi in low volume and good risk disease, and even Zanubrutinib in
MCL, as well as any data from these other trials, there are other aspects that need significant improvement as detailed
below.
Abstract
The abstract lacks any background which justifies the use of this therapy in this disease. Please add.
Please describe further the patient population. The description of ‘untreated MCL’ is insufficient.
Please define any acronyms used in the abstract eg “MCL”
Please explain further why 4 cycles of ‘R-DHAOX’ therapy is considered shortened therapy after the le Gouill LYMA study
used 4 cycles and only RCHOP14 in those in <PR.
The treatment paradigm is not completely clear in the abstract or the methods-do all patients get RDHAOX or only those in
‘cr’ or ‘pd’ included what if they reached the 12 cycles with SD or PR?-I know there were not any of these but clarification
would be helpful. Why do only those in CR get maintenance?
Please include the confidence interval for the CR rate.
Introduction.
Please provide more details about the regimens not just the name of the trials. The ‘Triangle regimen’ doesn’t exist, it is a
randomised trial with different regimens and no clear new standard, one arm assessed therapy with a BTKi, not
immunotherapy. Please amend.
Furthermore, these regimens and autograft are not suitable for all patients with MCL, so please clarify this and discuss.
It would be useful to provide information about the outcomes from the chemotherapy backbone the authors have chosen for
their study (RDHAOx), as this was not the standard therapy for the LyMA trial,
There is limited information on the data from Zanubrutinib in MCL in this introduction. Please refer to and discuss the
relevant information to provide jusfication of the use in frontline.
Methods:
please include a methods section after the introduction, rather than at the end, with the standard eligibility, enrolment
procedures, treatment details, assessments, statistics and methods of evaluation, the entire protocol can be included,
however the poignant information needs to be in the methods-the detailed sections on laboratory methods are less important
than the aforementioned requirements for a clinical trial. Why was an age of 75 chosen if patients are fit, and not being
transplanted.
Please define what ‘unacceptable toxicity’ is in terms of cessation of Part A.
Please clarify why patients in PR were taken off the study.
Please reference the statistical assumptions used in this trial.
Results:
1. It is unclear if the patient population is one that is transplant eligible or not, and although the upper age limit was 75, few
patients over 65 appear to have been enrolled, and whether it included those with non-measurable disease.
2. Why do the authors think there is such a high proportion in this study who are male? (83%), even with a male
predominance, this seems high.
3. Please state how many patients underwent PET, given the methods state PET or CT was used. Was CR confirmed with a
bone marrow biopsy as well as PET? And did such a high number really convert from PR to CR in 8 weeks having only
achieved a PR at cycle 2? It seems a little surprising.
4. Please clarify if all of the PD continued to 12months of R-zanu, or whether they progressed earlier and received RDHAOx.
5. Line 104 appears to be an error-the vs should be between the blastoid/classic categories.
6. Please include dose disruptions as well as dose reductions in the R-zanu group. If there was not dose reduction and Zanu
is continuous, how was the grade 3+ neutropenia managed in the 7% reported who had it. What was the management of
infection such as covid? Was there provision in the protocol for cessation? This study ran during the covid pandemic when
vaccination was not available, all other BTKi studies had significant issues with COVID yet it is not mentioned here.
7. Dose reductions of 82% for the chemo is extremely high for this regimen. Please comment on reasons, and details of the
dose reductions that occurred. Please include description of the GCSF use.
8. It would be useful to have the TP53 mutation status documented in the results of the manuscript – it is currently quite
difficult to find this in a supplementary figure. Was there any difference in response to treatment or outcomes for TP53
mutated vs wild type patients?
9. The frequency of TP53 mutation was lower than in other contemporary cohorts of MCL patients who have had WES
performed (typically 20-30%). This may have influenced the results.
10. Why were those requiring anticoagulants excluded from the trial? (point 4 under Exclusion Criteria in the protocol). In
clinical practice patients on anticoagulation therapy would be eligible to receive a BTKi
11. For MRD assessment, the authors state ‘bone marrow +/- peripheral blood’ was used. Please elaborate on how this was
decided or if it was at random. Not all patients had bone marrow involvement at baseline – did these patients have
detectable disease in peripheral blood and were these patients subsequently evaluated using peripheral blood?
12. In figure S5, the most common somatic mutation is OBSCN. Pathogenic mutations in the obscurin gene have not been
found in any lymphomas in online clinical databases, and are most often VUS or benign variants. Could the authors please
comment on their finding of OBSCN mutations in 29.7% of the cohort? Was there strong evidence for pathogenicity?
13. Although the results here are promising, the median follow up time is 23 months and perhaps too short to conclude that
there was a high rate of 'sustained' CR.
Discussion
The reference to the Lugano criteria should be in a methods section, not the discussion.
The authors have not discussed studies of BTKi in combination with rituximab, nor any of the R-bendamustine studies which
are relevant here due to the enrolment of patients up to age 75.
The limitations of the study need to be expanded, claims being made about differences in the molecular subgroups in the
absence of adequate power for any multivariable analysis need to be softened and noted in the limitations.
Why is 4 cycles of RDHAOX considered shortened in the conclusion, when it is given to patients mostly in CR?
General: there are numerous grammatical errors throughout the manuscript that are obvious to a native English speaker.
Although these do not always detract from the meaning of the phrase, they are noticeable and need to be rectified.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:

Pg2. The conclusion to the abstract should reflect the findings of a single arm phase II study. It overstates results to say the

the authors state: "Further randomized controlled trials should be conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the
proposed treatment regimen in this trial." This should be included in any concluding statement .

Reviewer #1
This clinical trial evaluated the efficacy of zanubrutinib-rituximab induction followed by a shortened
R-DHAOx chemoimmunotherapy and zanubrutinib maintenance regimen in previously untreated
mantle cell lymphoma patients. The study demonstrated a high complete response rate, durable
remission, and manageable toxicities. Additionally, the authors identified three transcriptome based
molecular subtypes that correlated with treatment response and survival outcomes. I would recommend
the publication in Nature Communications with the following major revisions.
Q1: The Abstract section would benefit from being streamlined to highlight the key points of this study
and to emphasize the advantages of this regimen as a frontline treatment for MCL patients.
Answer: Thank you for the valuable comment. We made the following revisions to the Abstract (Line 27-

Line 27-51:
Abstract
This multicenter, phase II trial evaluated zanubrutinib plus rituximab induction, followed by shortened
chemoimmunotherapy as frontline treatment for mantle cell lymphoma (MCL). Forty-two patients with
histologically confirmed, stage II-IV MCL requiring immediate anti-lymphoma treatment were enrolled.
Patients received zanubrutinib-rituximab regimen (part A) for up to 12 cycles; subjects achieving
complete response (CR) or disease progression proceeded to four cycles of R-DHAOx (rituximab,
dexamethasone, cytarabine and oxaliplatin) (part B). Patients with CR at part B completion received
zanubrutinib maintenance for one year. The primary endpoint was the CR rate at part A completion,
which was 88% (95% confidence interval [CI], 74-96). The CR rate at part B completion was 86% (95%
CI, 72-95). With the median follow-up of 23 months, the 2-year progression-free survival and overall
survival was 85% (95% CI, 75-97) and 90% (95% CI, 75-100), respectively. Toxicities were moderate in
part A; hematological adverse events were common in part B. In conclusion, zanubrutinib-rituximab
induction followed by shortened R-DHAOx is efficacious and safe as a frontline therapy for MCL. This
strategy allows for a reduction in chemotherapy cycles, and should be validated in future randomized
controlled trials. Clinical trial registration: NCT04624958.
Q2: In the Introduction section, please clarify the rationale for selecting R-DHAOx— typically used as
a salvage therapy or as first-line induction for younger lymphoma patients—as the shortened
chemoimmunotherapy component in this regimen.
Answer: We are grateful for your comment, and expanded the Introduction section to explain the rationale
for selecting R-DHAOx: (1) In the MCL Younger trial1, adding high-dose cytarabine to
immunochemotherapy increased the CR rate (55% for R-CHOP/R-DHAP vs 39% for R-CHOP). (2) R-
DHA-platinum regimen is one of the preferred regimens in the NCCN guideline with a high CR rate
(77%).2 (3) In the subgroup analyses of LyMa trial,3 there was a tendency for longer disease control
duration with oxaliplatin than cisplatin and carboplatin. (4) Overlapping toxicity of thrombocytopenia in
high-dose cytarabine and carboplatin, as well as lower nephrotoxicity and ease of administration of
oxaliplatin vs cisplatin.4,5
We have added relevant content in the Introduction (Line 91-101).
Line 91-101: To expand the potential use, we chose R-DHAOx (rituximab, dexamethasone, cytarabine,
and oxaliplatin), another commonly used cytarabine-based regimen in this trial. The R-DHAOx regimen
was selected for the following reasons: 1) The improved outcomes of adding high-dose cytarabine to
chemoimmunotherapy.27 2) R-DHA-platinum regimen is one of the preferred regimens in the National
Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guideline with a high CR rate (77%) in the LyMa trial.2 3) In
the subgroup analyses of LyMa trial, there was a tendency for longer disease control duration than
cisplatin and carboplatin.28 4) Given that the potential overlapping toxicity of thrombocytopenia in high-
dose cytarabine and carboplatin, as well as lower nephrotoxicity and ease of administration with
oxaliplatin than cisplatin,29,30 we chose oxaliplatin as the platinum used in our regimen.

receive consolidation with ASCT and/or maintenance therapy. Patients with PR are recommended to
receive further chemoimmunotherapy or covalent BTKi if not exposed to covalent BTKi previously (not

treatment, or if continued treatment is deemed inappropriate by the investigators.

Usually, previous trials of MCL defined an upper age of 65 years for patients suitable for ASCT and

Line 373-393: Responses were evaluated by the investigators every two cycles in part A and part B, and
every three cycles during maintenance therapy using PET or computerized tomography (CT) according
to the Lugano 2014 criteria.32 A bone marrow biopsy is required to confirm CR in patients with bone
marrow involvement at baseline. Safety assessment was performed upon all patient visits. Adverse
events (AEs) were graded according to the National Cancer Institute’s Common Terminology Criteria for
Adverse Events (version 5.0).
MRD in bone marrow and/or peripheral blood were measured using flow cytometry with a
sensitivity of 10-4 at baseline and upon the completion of part A and part B. Bone marrow aspiration was
performed at completion of part A and part B in patients with bone marrow involvement at baseline but
not routinely in patients without bone marrow involvement at baseline. The collection of peripheral
blood for MRD evaluation was performed at baseline and upon the completion of part A and part B.
Detectable MRD in either bone marrow or peripheral blood was considered MRD-positive.
The primary endpoint was the CR rate at the completion of part A in the intention-to-treat
population, defined as proportion of patients with CR. Secondary endpoints included overall response
(proportion of patients with CR plus PR), MRD, PFS, OS, and adverse events for part A, part B and
maintenance phase. PFS was defined as the time from treatment initiation to disease progression or
death, whichever occurs earlier, and was censored at the last follow-up date in alive patients without
disease progression. OS was defined as the time from treatment initiation to patient death or the last
follow-up.

patients.
Response assessment was performed in the full analysis set (ITT population) and per protocol set.
Safety assessment was performed in the safety analysis set, which was divided into three datasets and
each contained patients who received the study treatment at least once in part A, part B, or maintenance
phase.
Descriptive statistics were used to present baseline characteristics, response rates, and rate of AEs.
The 95% confidence interval (CI) of rates was calculated using the Clopper-Pearson method. Survival
outcomes and 95% CIs were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. The 2-year PFS and OS were
calculated. The log-rank test was used to evaluate the difference in PFS and OS between subgroups.
Post-hoc analyses included the subgroup analyses of CR rate at part A completion, CR rate at part B
completion, PFS, and OS. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 25.0) and R
software (version 3.6.1). Two-sided P of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

rituximab regimen), late-CR (achieving CR after more than four cycles of zanubrutinib-rituximab
regimen), and non-CR. Bulk RNA-sequencing was conducted and samples were classified into three

burden. Detailed methods of RNA sequencing and WES are presented in the supplementary materials.

Q3: Please clarify why patients in PR were taken off the study.
Answer: Thank you for raising this critical point. The design that only patients achieving CR proceeded
to maintenance) was based on the NCCN guideline: (1) For patients receiving aggressive induction therapy,
only CR patients are recommended to receive consolidation with ASCT and/or maintenance therapy.
Patients with PR are recommended to receive further chemoimmunotherapy or covalent BTKi if not
exposed to covalent BTKi previously (not applicable to the current study population). (2) For patients
receiving less-aggressive induction therapy, CR and PR patients could consider maintenance therapy with
rituximab; and for PR patients, they could also receive further chemoimmunotherapy or covalent BTKi.
In summary, we did not impose restrictions on the subsequent therapies for patients with PR; instead,
they taken off the trial to ensure receiving optimal and individualized treatment. Therefore, only CR
patients got maintenance.

Q4: Please reference the statistical assumptions used in this trial.

to the text (Line 475-478), which was based on the results of the LyMA trial.1 The LyMa trial reported a
CR rate of 41% (124/299) and an unconfirmed CR rate of 36% (107/299) after R-DHA-platinum induction.
However, there are still some differences compared with the current trial: 1) In the LyMa trial,
carboplatin, and oxaliplatin were used in 76 and 38 patients, respectively; the remainder received cisplatin.
In contrast, all subjects in the current study received oxaliplatin; 2) Efficacy was evaluated using the 1999
International Working Group criteria in the LyMa trial versus the Lugano 2014 criteria in the current study.
Accordingly, unconfirmed CR was included in the CR rate in the LyMa trial but not the current study; 3)

In sample size estimation, we roughly took the number of patients achieving CR (n=124) or CRu
(n=107) in the LyMA trial, minus the number of patients who received R-CHOP due to inadequate response
(n=20), resulting in approximately 70% (211/299).

Q1: It is unclear if the patient population is one that is transplant eligible or not, and although the upper
age limit was 75, few patients over 65 appear to have been enrolled, and whether it included those with
non-measurable disease.
Answer: Thank you for raising these important points.
(1) Transplant eligibility:
In the current trial, we did not set strict criteria for eligibility for transplantation. According to the study
design, the ASCT was only used for patients aged ≤ 65 years with positive MRD at part B completion.
Eventually, no patient underwent ASCT because all the CR patients who proceeded to part B achieved
MRD negativity, obviating the need for transplant.
(2) Age distribution:
The patients in the current study were indeed younger than that in several clinical trials without age limit,1-
3 as well as several real-world studies in MCL patients.4-6 First, First, since the age was set between 18 and
75 years, so patients over 75 were not included, resulting in a relatively low proportion of patients aged 65
and older. Second, during patient recruitment, there was a tendency for older patients to refuse to participate
when they learned chemotherapeutic drugs are used in part B of the trial.
(3) Measurable disease:
For enrollment, all patients were required to have at least one measurable lesion (Line 337-341).

Q6: Please include dose disruptions as well as dose reductions in the R-zanu group. If there was not
dose reduction and Zanu is continuous, how was the grade 3+ neutropenia managed in the 7% reported
who had it. What was the management of infection such as covid? Was there provision in the protocol
for cessation? This study ran during the covid pandemic when vaccination was not available, all other
BTKi studies had significant issues with COVID yet it is not mentioned here.
Answer: We deeply appreciated for this valuable comment, and added detailed description of dose
suspension/reduction during the trial period (Line 180-183, Line 188-202, and Line 203-206). According
to the protocol, grade 3-4 hematological toxicities required a treatment suspension until recovery to ≤ grade
1, with zanubrutinib maintained at 160mg BID during zanubrutinib-rituximab treatment. Dose reduction
to 80mg BID was implemented only upon recurrence of the same toxicity. In our study, three patients (7%)
experienced grade 3-4 neutropenia for once; therefore, none needed dose reductions.
Thank you for highlighting this critical aspect of trial conduct during the pandemic. With regards to
the COVID-19 issue, only one patient death was attributed to COVID-19, presumably due to relatively
strict preventive measures in China.
(1) The management of SARS-CoV-2 infection during pandemic: All patients underwent
mandatory SARS-CoV-2 PCR testing prior to hospitalization between 2020 and 2023. Outpatients
receiving zanubrutinib at home were tested immediately if they developed fever or respiratory symptoms.
In patients with positive result, all anti-lymphoma treatments were suspended and patients received
immediate COVID-directed therapy. Anti-lymphoma treatment resumed only after complete recovery (two
consecutive negative PCR tests at least 24 h apart). Routine screening before hospitalization was
discontinued after 2023. However, all patients developing fever (≥ 38℃), cough, dyspnea, or new hypoxia
would still underwent prompt PCR testing.
(2) Provision in the protocol for cessation: Measures for SARS-CoV-2-related cessation rule was
not included in the trial protocol, but decided by the investigators.
(3) SARS-CoV-2-related information in our trial: A total of 30 patients tested positive for SARS-
CoV-2, and treatment was suspended in 17 patients. One patient died due to SARS-CoV-2. The Results
section has been expanded to describe these findings (Line 208-211).

Q10: Why were those requiring anticoagulants excluded from the trial? (point 4 under Exclusion
Criteria in the protocol). In clinical practice patients on anticoagulation therapy would be eligible to
receive a BTKi
Answer: We agree that anticoagulation therapy does not represent a contraindication for BTKi treatment
in clinical practice. However, hemorrhage events are frequent in patients with B-cell malignancies treated
with BTKi (ibrutinib as well as 2nd generation BTKis like zanubrutinib).1 Supporting evidence mainly
comes from a phase II trial of zanubrutinib in relapsed/refractory MCL2, where hemorrhage events
occurred in 25.6% of patients and major hemorrhage was reported in 3 patients (3.5%), including one with
cerebral hemorrhage and two with gastrointestinal hemorrhages. Consequently, the zanubrutinib
prescription information explicitly warns that coadministration of zanubrutinib with antiplatelet or
anticoagulant medications may further increase the risk of hemorrhage
(https://www.brukinsa.com/prescribing-information.pdf). Based on these concerns, we excluded patients
who require anticoagulants from the current trial. Similar design has been used in most BTKi-containing
clinical trials in MCL, eg. the SHINE trial3, the ECHO trial4, and the WINDOW-1 trial5.

Cell Lymphoma. N Engl J Med. 2022;386(26):2482-2494.
4. Wang M, Salek D, Belada D, et al. Acalabrutinib Plus Bendamustine-Rituximab in Untreated Mantle Cell
Lymphoma. J Clin Oncol. 2025;43(20):2276-2284.
5. Wang ML, Jain P, Zhao S, et al. Ibrutinib-rituximab followed by R-HCVAD as frontline treatment for
young patients (≤65 years) with mantle cell lymphoma (WINDOW-1): a single-arm, phase 2 trial. Lancet
Oncol. 2022;23(3):406-415.
Q11: For MRD assessment, the authors state ‘bone marrow +/- peripheral blood’ was used. Please
elaborate on how this was decided or if it was at random. Not all patients had bone marrow involvement
at baseline – did these patients have detectable disease in peripheral blood and were these patients
subsequently evaluated using peripheral blood?
Answer: We appreciate for this suggestion. In our trial, for patients with bone marrow involvement at
baseline, a bone marrow aspiration was performed for MRD detection at completion of part A and part B.
For patients without bone marrow involvement at baseline, bone marrow aspiration was not routinely
performed. The collection of peripheral blood for MRD evaluation was performed at baseline and upon
the completion of part A and part B.
MRD assessment deviated from the plan during the trial process in some patients refused sample
collection of bone marrow or peripheral blood, which in turn led to discrepancies in the number of available
MRD results. We added the sample collection protocol/rules for MRD assessment in Methods (Line 381-
385) and specific collection at each time point in annotation of Table S1.
In the six patients without bone marrow involvement at baseline, none had detectable MRD in
peripheral blood; these patients were evaluated subsequently using peripheral blood for MRD. The Results
section has been revised to describe these facts (Line 118-120).
Line 381-385: Bone marrow aspiration was performed at completion of part A and part B in patients with
bone marrow involvement at baseline but not routinely in patients without bone marrow involvement at
baseline. The collection of peripheral blood for MRD evaluation was performed at baseline and upon the
completion of part A and part B.
Table S1:
Line 118-120: In the six patients without bone marrow involvement at baseline, none had detectable
MRD in peripheral blood, and they underwent MRD detection only in peripheral blood in subsequent
time points.
Q12: In figure S5, the most common somatic mutation is OBSCN. Pathogenic mutations in the obscurin
gene have not been found in any lymphomas in online clinical databases, and are most often VUS or
benign variants. Could the authors please comment on their finding of OBSCN mutations in 29.7% of
the cohort? Was there strong evidence for pathogenicity?
Answer: We appreciate for this important comment, and updated WES analysis by further including 12
negative control samples (bringing the total to 23 cases with negative control samples). Additionally, the
review of the WES results in last version of manuscript showed a large number of low-abundance, splice
variants, which were inconsistent with actual conditions. Consequently, we increased the threshold for
somatic mutation calling from 3 reads to 4 reads for all the genes. The detailed methods have been revised
in the supplementary methods.
In the updated analysis, the mutation rate of OBSCN was 10.8% (Figure S6), including missense
mutations in four patients: c.556G>A(p.A186T), c.2765C>T(p.T922M), c.2997_2998inv(p.A1000T), and
c.20648G>C(p.R6883P). The somatic mutation of OBSCN was uncommon in MCL in most of previous
studies, but a recent genomic study reported 5% OBSCN mutation rate among 123 newly-diagnosed MCL
patients.1 Then we compared the expression level of OBCSN between patients with versus without OBSCN
mutation based on RNAseq (figure below), but found no significant differences. For response and survival
outcomes, patients with OBSCN mutation had a CR rate of 50% (2/4), and an inferior PFS than those
without mutation, but no difference in OS (figures below).
Taken together, based on the current findings, no conclusions can be drawn regarding the clinical and
pathogenic value of OBSCN mutations in MCL.

1. Yi S, Yan Y, Jin M, et al. Genomic and transcriptomic profiling reveals distinct molecular subsets
associated with outcomes in mantle cell lymphoma. J Clin Invest. 2022;132(3):e153283.
Q13: Although the results here are promising, the median follow up time is 23 months and perhaps too
short to conclude that there was a high rate of 'sustained' CR.
Answer: Thank you for this suggestion. We refrained from claiming “sustained CR” in the revised
manuscript (Line 326-328).
Line 326-328: In conclusion, zanubrutinib-rituximab induction followed by a shortened R-DHAOx
chemoimmunotherapy and maintenance with zanubrutinib as the frontline treatment resulted in a high
rate of sustained CR in patients with untreated MCL.
Discussion:
Q1: The reference to the Lugano criteria should be in a methods section, not the discussion.
Answer: We appreciate for the comment, and added reference citation to the Lugano criteria to the
Methods section (Line 373-376).
Line 373-376: Responses were evaluated by the investigators every two cycles in part A and part B, and
every three cycles during maintenance therapy using PET or computerized tomography (CT) according
to the Lugano 2014 criteria.32
Q2: The authors have not discussed studies of BTKi in combination with rituximab, nor any of the R-
bendamustine studies which are relevant here due to the enrolment of patients up to age 75.
Answer: We are grateful for this suggestion, and expanded the Discussion section to address combination
of BTKi with rituximab, bendamustine-rituximab with or without BTKi (ibrutinib or acalabrutinib) (Line
287-297). Also, a comprehensive comparison with the WINDOW-1 trial, which was similar in study design
to our trial, has already been provided (Line 267-286).
Line 287-297: A recent phase II trial reported 80% CR rate when using the ibrutinib-rituximab regimen
in treating untreated indolent clinical forms of MCL (non-blastoid variants, Ki-67 ≤ 30%, asymptomatic
disease, ECOG 0-1, and largest lesion diameter ≤ 3cm).16 Five out of 42 patients in the current trial had
untreated indolent clinical forms of MCL using the same criteria and all achieved CR. In addition, our
trial included nine patients 65-75 years of age, and achieved a CR rate of 88% in this group of patients.
In previous trials for MCL patients of 65 years of age or older, ibrutinib-rituximab regimen resulted in a
CR rate of 71%,17 whereas the CR rate in patients receiving BR regimen with or without BTK inhibitors
(ibrutinib or acalabrutinib) was 65.5%-66.6% and 53.5%-57.6%.8,35 A phase II trial investigating BR plus
low-dose cytarabine regimen in MCL patients aged > 65 years or 60-65 years but ineligible for
HDT/ASCT reported a CR rate of 91% at the end of treatment.36
Line 267-286: Compared to the WINDOW-1 trial,21 patients in this trial had numerically higher
percentage of Ki-67 ≥ 30%, higher MIPI risk, but lower rate of TP53 mutation. The duration of induction
treatment was also shorter in this trial (median cycles: 4 vs 7). Despite these differences, the response to
zanubrutinib-rituximab induction in this trial (CR, 88%; ORR, 98%) was similar to that reported for
ibrutinib plus rituximab in the WINDOW-1 trial (CR, 87%; ORR, 98%). The fewer cycles needed to
achieve CR in this trial may reflect improved efficacy; alternatively, this difference may be attributable to
the fact that responses were assessed using PET scans routinely after cycle 4 in this trial but only used to
verify CR after CT screening in the WINDOW-1 trial. Temporal pattern of treatment failure also differed:
all five PD events in this trial occurred within nine months of treatment initiation; in contrast, the PD
events in the WINDOW-1 trial occurred over a much longer period, even after 24 months. This
difference might be related to the maintenance therapy with zanubrutinib following
chemoimmunotherapy in our trial, but an extended follow-up is warranted since the median follow-up
was only 23 months.
None of the patients in this trial required dose reduction of zanubrutinib during zanubrutinib-
rituximab induction treatment. In contrast, one third of patients in the WINDOW-1 trial required dose
reduction of ibrutinib due to AEs. Such a difference may reflect a more favorable safety profile with the
zanubrutinib-rituximab regimen than ibrutinib plus rituximab. Additionally, this difference could also be
attributable to the shorter induction cycles in our trial.
Q3: The limitations of the study need to be expanded, claims being made about differences in the
molecular subgroups in the absence of adequate power for any multivariable analysis need to be
softened and noted in the limitation.
Answer: Thank you for this suggestion. We expanded the limitation section to included likely confounding
by molecular subgroups in the absence of adequate power for multivariable analysis (Line 323-325).
Line 323-325: Third, in the molecular subtype analyses, the absence of multivariable analysis and
independent validation has resulted in a reduced reliability of the findings, necessitating further
verification.
Q4: Why is 4 cycles of RDHAOX considered shortened in the conclusion, when it is given to patients
mostly in CR?
Answer: We appreciate your insightful comment, and wish to explain that the word "shortened" is used in
the manuscript in the context of most of the cytarabine-based chemotherapy regimens, such as the 6
alternating cycles of R-maxiCHOP/ R+high-dose cytarabine (Nordic regimen)1, 6 alternating cycles of R-
CHOP/R-DHAP2,3, 6-8 alternating cycles of R+hyper-CVAD/R+high dose methotrexate and cytarabine4,
6 alternating cycles of R+bendamustine/R+high-dose cytarabine5.
Although the LyMa trial6 also utilized 4 cycles of R-DHAP, the intensity of the overall treatment was
ensured by (1) a routine consolidation therapy with HDT+ASCT for all patients; (2) an additional rescue
induction therapy with 4 cycles of R-CHOP-14 for patients with PR and whose tumor mass had been
reduced by less than 75%; (3) 1 cycle of CVP regimen was allowed to reduce tumor burden before R-
DHAP according to local investigator decision.
In our study, we anticipated to use a chemo-free induction (zanubrutinib-rituximab) and maintenance
(zanubrutinib) to minimize the use of cytotoxic chemotherapy drugs and HDT/ASCT. At the completion
of part B, all the CR patients were MRD-negative, and were not consolidated with HDT/ASCT. Therefore,
compared to the LyMa trial, the treatment intensity in our trial was decreased by using mild induction and
maintenance therapies.
The Discussion section of the manuscript has been revised to reflects these thoughts (Line 244-252).
Line 244-252: Currently, most of the cytarabine-based chemotherapy regimens, such as the NORDIC
regimen10, alternating R-CHOP/R-DHAP regimen4,30, and R-hyper-CVAD/R-high dose methotrexate and
cytarabine regimen31, contain six to eight cycles of treatment. The current trial used a shortened four cycles
of R-DHAOx regimen. Notably, the LyMa trial2 also used four cycles of R-DHAP, but the intensity of the
overall treatment was ensured by routine consolidation therapy with HDT/ASCT, additional four cycles of
R-CHOP for PR patients, and one cycle of CVP regimen was allowed before study treatment. The
treatment intensity was lower in the current study due to mild chemotherapy-free induction and
maintenance therapy to minimize the use of cytotoxic chemotherapy drugs and HDT/ASCT.
Reference:
1. Eskelund CW, Kolstad A, Jerkeman M, et al. 15-year follow-up of the Second Nordic Mantle Cell
Lymphoma trial (MCL2): prolonged remissions without survival plateau. Br J Haematol.
2016;175(3):410-418.
2. Dreyling M, Doorduijn J, Giné E, et al. Ibrutinib combined with immunochemotherapy with or without
autologous stem-cell transplantation versus immunochemotherapy and autologous stem-cell
transplantation in previously untreated patients with mantle cell lymphoma (TRIANGLE): a three-arm,
randomised, open-label, phase 3 superiority trial of the European Mantle Cell Lymphoma Network.
Lancet. 2024;403(10441):2293-2306.
3. Hermine O, Hoster E, Walewski J, et al. Addition of high-dose cytarabine to immunochemotherapy
before autologous stem-cell transplantation in patients aged 65 years or younger with mantle cell
lymphoma (MCL Younger): a randomised, open-label, phase 3 trial of the European Mantle Cell
Lymphoma Network. Lancet. 2016;388(10044):565-575.
4. Romaguera JE. et al. High rate of durable remissions after treatment of newly diagnosed aggressive
mantle-cell lymphoma with rituximab plus hyper-CVAD alternating with rituximab plus high-dose
methotrexate and cytarabine. J Clin Oncol. 2005;23(28):7013-7023.
5. Merryman RW, Edwin N, Redd R, et al. Rituximab/bendamustine and rituximab/cytarabine induction
therapy for transplant-eligible mantle cell lymphoma. Blood Adv. 2020;4(5):858-867.
6. Le Gouill S, Thieblemont C, Oberic L, et al. Rituximab after Autologous Stem-Cell Transplantation in
Mantle-Cell Lymphoma. N Engl J Med. 2017;377(13):1250-1260.
General:
Q1: there are numerous grammatical errors throughout the manuscript that are obvious to a native
English speaker. Although these do not always detract from the meaning of the phrase, they are
noticeable and need to be rectified.
Answer: During the revision, we worked with a professional medical editor (Kehong Zhang, M.D., Ph.D.,
from the Ivy Medical Editing; formerly an Assistant Professor at the Harvard Medical School) to improve
language readability.
Reviewer #4 (Biostats):
The multicenter, phase II trial (CHESS) evaluated zanubrutinib plus rituximab induction, followed by
shortened chemoimmunotherapy in untreated MCL patients. The primary endpoint was the CR rate
achieved after induction. Overall the report is clear and comprehensive and focussed on the primary
and secondary endpoints. There is some interesting exploratory analysis included which adds to the
impact of the work.
I have a number of fairly minor points that I believe should be addressed to improve the clarity of
presentation.
Q1: Pg2. In the abstract please report estimates (CR rate, PFS and OS rate) with appropriate confidence
intervals as per journal guidelines.
Answer: We appreciate this comment, and added 95% confidence intervals (Line 35-37 and Line 38-39).
Line 35-37: The primary endpoint was the CR rate at part A completion, which was 88% (95%
confidence interval [CI], 74-96). The CR rate at part B completion was 86% (95% CI, 72-95).
Line 38-39: With the median follow-up of 23 months, the 2-year progression-free survival and overall
survival was 85% (95% CI, 75-97) and 90% (95% CI, 75-100), respectively.
Q2: Pg2. The conclusion to the abstract should reflect the findings of a single arm phase II study. It
overstates results to say the treatment is "effective and safe" without indicating he further evaluation
required in phase III. For example, in the discussion the authors state: "Further randomized controlled
trials should be conducted to evaluate the efficacy and safety of the proposed treatment regimen in this
trial." This should be included in any concluding statement .
Answer: We are grateful for your valuable comment, and revised the conclusion part of Abstract (Line 47-
51) as well as the Discussion (Line 326-331).
Line 47-51: In conclusion, zanubrutinib-rituximab induction followed by shortened R-DHAOx is
efficacious and safe as a frontline therapy for MCL. This strategy allows for a reduction in chemotherapy
cycles, and should be validated in future randomized controlled trials.
Line 326-331: In conclusion, zanubrutinib-rituximab induction followed by a shortened R-DHAOx
chemoimmunotherapy and maintenance with zanubrutinib as the frontline treatment resulted in a high
rate of CR in patients with untreated MCL. The induction phase and maintenance phase were well-
tolerated; however, significant myelosuppression was still observed during the chemoimmunotherapy
phase. Future randomized controlled trials are required to validate strategies that minimize chemotherapy
use in first line treatment of MCL.
Q3: Pg5. Please add more detail on treatment delivered including dose modification required and delays
between cycles. If they did not occur, please state as such --- I note that comment in the Discussion on
page 8. For example, the protocol states: "The exposure time and dose of experimental drug therapy
were summarized. List the number of patients for whom the dose was adjusted/suspended, along with
the reasons for the dose adjustment/suspension." Please report this information appropriately, as
required.
Answer: We deeply appreciated for this valuable comment, and added detailed description of dose
suspension/reduction during the trial period (Line 180-183, Line 188-202, and Line 203-206). According
to the protocol, grade 3-4 hematological toxicities required a treatment suspension until recovery to ≤ grade
1, with zanubrutinib maintained at 160mg BID during zanubrutinib-rituximab treatment. Dose reduction
to 80mg BID was implemented only upon recurrence of the same toxicity. In our study, three patients (7%)
experienced grade 3-4 neutropenia once; therefore, none needed dose reductions.
Line 180-183: No patient needed zanubrutinib dose reduction in part A. Zanubrutinib dose suspension
was required in five (12%) of 42 patients (three patients for neutropenia, one for infection, and one for
elevated liver enzymes).
Line 188-202: Dose reduction of chemotherapeutic agents was required in 32 (82%) of 39 patients due to
toxicities (27 patients for thrombocytopenia, four for neutropenia, and one for elevated liver enzymes).
Of these, 25 patients had their dose of cytarabine reduced by one dose level to 75% of the original dose,
and seven patients required a reduction of two dose levels to 50%. Five patients were still unable to
tolerate thrombocytopenia after dose reduction and discontinued part B treatment. Thrombopoietin
receptor agonists (TPO-RAs) or recombinant human thrombopoietin (rhTPO) were given in 9 patients as
primary prevention for thrombocytopenia, and in 13 patients as secondary prevention. Recombinant
human granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (rhG-CSF) was given in 26 patients as primary prevention
for neutropenia, and in all the 19 patients who had experienced grade 3-4 neutropenia as secondary
prevention. Chemotherapy dose suspension was required in 20 (51%) of 39 patients due to toxicities (18
patients for thrombocytopenia, one for neutropenia, and one for elevated liver enzymes).
Line 203-206: One patient needed zanubrutinib dose reduction to 80 mg twice a day due to grade 3
neutropenia. Zanubrutinib dose suspension was required in six (18%) of 34 patients (two patients for
neutropenia, two patients for fatigue, and one patient each for thrombocytopenia and infections).
Line 208-211: This trial was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic. One patient died from COVID-
19 pneumonia and respiratory failure during part B. A total of 30 patients tested positive for SARS-CoV-
2 at least once, and 17 patients required treatment suspension due to SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Q4: Pg 10. The conclusion should reflect the aims and have a mention of safety also. Please add.
Answer: We appreciate the comments and added safety to the conclusion (Line 326-331).
Line 326-331: In conclusion, zanubrutinib-rituximab induction followed by a shortened R-DHAOx
chemoimmunotherapy and maintenance with zanubrutinib as the frontline treatment resulted in a high
rate of CR in patients with untreated MCL. The induction phase and maintenance phase were well-
tolerated; however, significant myelosuppression was still observed during the chemoimmunotherapy
phase. Future randomized controlled trials are required to validate strategies that minimize chemotherapy
use in first line treatment of MCL.
Q5: Pg 10. Describe who was blinded or not. For example, participants and clinician not blinded. Was
outcome assessor blinded?
Answer: This was an open-label trial. Participants, investigators, attending physicians and outcome
assessors were not blinded. We apologize for not making it clear in the original manuscript, and revised
the Methods accordingly (Line 336-337).
Line 336-337: This was an open-label trial. Participants, investigators, attending physicians and outcome
assessors were not blinded.
Q6:Pg 11/14. Please define the ITT, PAS and safety population more clearly in statistical analysis section
and ensure this refects what is stated in the protocol and how analysing was undertaken.
Answer: We appreciate the comment, and added term definitions to the statistical analysis section (Line
479-491 and Line 390-393).
Line 479-491: Response assessment was performed in the full analysis set (ITT population) and per
protocol set. Safety assessment was performed in the safety analysis sets, which was divided into three
datasets and each contained patients who received the study treatment at least once in part A, part B, or
maintenance phase.
Descriptive statistics were used to present baseline characteristics, response rates, and rate of AEs.
The 95% confidence interval (CI) of rates was calculated using the Clopper-Pearson method. Survival
outcomes and 95% CIs were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. The 2-year PFS and OS were
calculated. The log-rank test was used to evaluate the difference in PFS and OS between subgroups.
Post-hoc analyses included the subgroup analyses of CR rate at part A completion, CR rate at part B
completion, PFS, and OS. Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (version 25.0) and R
software (version 3.6.1). Two-sided P of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
Line 390-393: PFS was defined as the time from treatment initiation to disease progression or death,
whichever occurs earlier, and was censored at the last follow-up date in alive patients without disease
progression. OS was defined as the time from treatment initiation to patient death or the last follow-up.
Q7:Pg 14. Please clarify if the 5% type-one error is one-sided or two-sided. Fuurthemore, if it is one-
sided please clarify the impact this has on the confidence intervals you should report for the primary
endpoint.
Answer: Thank you for your helpful suggestions. We revised the Methods section to clearly state the the
5% type-one error was two-sided (Line 475-478).
Line 475-478: Sample size was estimated according to a single-stage phase 2 design based on the
following assumptions: 1) CR rate of 70% for historical control2 and 90% with the regimen in this trial;
2) 90% power and two-sided 5% type I error; 3) a dropout rate of 10%. The calculation yielded 42
patients.
